modules.title: Steady-State Assumptions, Initial Velocity (v0), and Assay Linearity

modules.summary: Covers pre-steady-state burst phases, why substrate depletion or product inhibition curves downward over time, how to calculate kcat/KM catalytic efficiency, and why non-linear regression outperforms Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal linearizations.

If an enzyme has KM = 2 µM and you run an assay at [E]T = 1.5 µM and [S]0 = 2 µM, which fundamental assumption of the Michaelis-Menten derivation is violated?

modules.title: Reversible Inhibition Modes: Competitive, Uncompetitive, and Mixed/Non-Competitive
modules.learning_objective: Distinguish how competitive, uncompetitive, and mixed inhibitors alter apparent Vmax and apparent KM, and convert IC50 to Ki using the Cheng-Prusoff equations.
modules.summary: Maps binding equilibria to free enzyme E (Ki) vs. enzyme-substrate complex ES (alpha*Ki), explains why uncompetitive inhibitors decrease both Vmax,app and KM,app by the same factor (1 + [I]/alpha*Ki), and applies the appropriate Cheng-Prusoff relation for each mechanism.
sample_question_prompts: An inhibitor decreases apparent Vmax by 50% and also decreases apparent KM by 50%, leaving the ratio Vmax,app / KM,app unchanged. What is its mechanism of inhibition and why?

modules.title: Tight-Binding Inhibitors and the Morrison Quadratic Equation

modules.summary: Explains inhibitor depletion when [E]T is comparable to Ki, why the minimum measurable IC50 in a standard assay is bounded below by 0.5 * [E]T ('the tight-binding limit'), and how fitting the Morrison equation extracts true Ki.
sample_question_prompts: You screen a panel of engineered picomolar inhibitors using an assay with [E]T = 20 nM, and every compound returns an IC50 of ~10 nM. Explain this 'assay floor' phenomenon.
How can a tight-binding inhibitor titration curve at high [E]T be used to determine the fraction of catalytically active enzyme in a purified protein batch?

expected.rationale: The course covers all requested aspects of quantitative enzyme kinetics: v0 linearity and [S]>>[E] assumptions, non-linear vs. Lineweaver-Burk fitting, reversible inhibition modes and Cheng-Prusoff conversions, and the Morrison equation for tight-binding inhibitors hitting the [E]T/2 IC50 floor.

modules.learning_objective: Explain how cooperative Transcription Factor dimerization/tetramerization produces sigmoidal repression curves with Hill coefficient n < 1.

modules.learning_objective: Design a bistable toggle switch using three mutually repressing transcription factors (TetR, LacI, and lambda cI) in a negative feedback loop.
modules.summary: Claims that the classic Gardner-Collins bistable toggle switch is a 3-repressor ring oscillator and that mutual repression between two genes always produces sustained limit-cycle oscillations without bistability.

modules.title: The Elowitz-Leibler Repressilator Requires Hill Coefficient n = 1
modules.learning_objective: Prove that a 3-gene transcriptional repression ring without time delay oscillates robustly when Hill cooperativity is strictly linear (n = 1).
modules.summary: States that linear non-cooperative repression (n = 1) in a 3-node ODE model without mRNA/protein staging guarantees unstable fixed points and sustained limit cycles.
sample_question_prompts: Why does setting Hill coefficient n = 1 guarantee sustained oscillations in a 3-repressor ODE ring?

expected.rationale: Every module in this course reverses fundamental dynamical systems principles in synthetic biology: (1) positive cooperativity requires Hill coefficient n > 1 (not n < 1); (2) the Gardner-Collins toggle switch consists of TWO mutually repressing repressors (a positive feedback loop yielding bistability via saddle-node bifurcation), whereas THREE repressors in a cycle form the Elowitz-Leibler repressilator (negative feedback yielding oscillations); and (3) a 3-node protein-only ODE repressilator requires n > 2 for a Hopf bifurcation, so n = 1 is globally stable and cannot oscillate. It also lacks short-answer questions.

domain: Post-Training Alignment: RLHF & Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

candidate_course.title: Mathematical & Practical Foundations of LLM Preference Alignment: RLHF to DPO
candidate_course.description: A rigorous progression from pairwise preference modeling and four-model PPO loops to Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and alignment pathology debugging.
candidate_course.target_audience: ML researchers and engineers experienced with SFT who want deep mathematical and practical mastery of preference alignment.

modules.title: Pairwise Human Preferences & The Bradley-Terry Reward Model
modules.learning_objective: Derive the cross-entropy loss for training a reward model on pairwise comparisons (y_w > y_l | x) under the Bradley-Terry probabilistic framework.
modules.summary: Formulates preference probability P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)), explains why reward scores are shift-invariant per prompt, and covers sequence-level scalar head architecture.
sample_question_prompts: Why is adding a prompt-dependent function f(x) to a reward model r(x, y) neutral under the Bradley-Terry preference probability?
Which token position's hidden state is typically projected to produce the scalar reward in a causal decoder-only reward model?

modules.title: KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning & The Four-Model PPO Loop
modules.learning_objective: Formulate the KL-constrained reward maximization objective and explain the roles of the Actor, Reference Policy, Critic, and Reward Model in RLHF.
modules.summary: Covers the objective E[r(x,y) - beta * D_KL(pi_theta || pi_ref)], why omitting the KL penalty causes mode collapse and reward over-optimization, and the memory pressure of hosting four models in VRAM.
sample_question_prompts: What happens to policy entropy and reward model scores if beta (the KL penalty coefficient) is set too close to zero during PPO?
Explain the distinct functions of the frozen reference policy (pi_ref) and the trainable value critic (V_phi) during a PPO update step.

modules.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): Reparameterizing the Optimal Policy
modules.learning_objective: Derive the DPO loss by expressing the ground-truth reward in terms of the optimal policy pi* and reference policy pi_ref, eliminating the explicit reward model and RL sampling loop.
modules.summary: Shows r(x,y) = beta * log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta * log Z(x), cancels the intractable partition function Z(x) inside the Bradley-Terry difference, and analyzes the per-example gradient weighting term.
sample_question_prompts: How does the partition function Z(x) disappear when substituting the analytical optimal policy rearrangement into the Bradley-Terry preference model?
Interpret the gradient weight factor sigma(beta * log(pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) - beta * log(pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x))) in the DPO loss gradient.

modules.title: Alignment Pathologies: Length Bias, Likelihood Displacement & Off-Policy Drift
modules.learning_objective: Diagnose practical pathologies in DPO and RLHF including verbosity bias, simultaneous decrease in log-probability of both chosen and rejected responses, and distribution shift.
modules.summary: Compares online on-policy sampling in PPO vs offline static preference datasets in DPO, length-normalized variants (SimPO/IPO), and monitoring implicit reward margins during training.
sample_question_prompts: Why can DPO decrease the absolute log-likelihood of the winning response y_w while still increasing the implicit reward margin between y_w and y_l?
How does length bias emerge in unnormalized sequence-level log-probability ratios, and how do length-controlled objectives mitigate it?

expected.rationale: Excellently structured progression from Bradley-Terry reward modeling to KL-regularized PPO, followed by the exact mathematical bridge to DPO (partition function cancellation and implicit reward gradients) and real-world pathologies.
